At constant temperature **PV = constant**, so the P-V graph is a **rectangular
hyperbola**.
**Step 1 — state the gas law.**
PV = nRT ✓
With n and T fixed, **PV = constant** - Boyle's law.
**Step 2 — see the shape.**
P = constant/V ✓ so P falls as V rises, steeply at small V and ever more gently at
large V, approaching both axes without ever touching them.
**Step 3 — identify the graph.** That is **Graph IV**, the hyperbola ✓
**Why not the straight falling line.** Graph III shows P decreasing **linearly** with
V ✓ But a linear fall would mean PV is **not** constant: at V = 1 and 2 with P = 4 and
3, the products are 4 and 6 - not an isotherm.
**The test that settles it.** Pick any two points and check that **PV is the same** ✓
On a hyperbola, doubling V exactly **halves** P. On a straight line it does not.
**Why the curve never touches the axes.** P → ∞ as V → 0 and P → 0 as V → ∞ ✓ Both
axes are **asymptotes** - infinite pressure would be needed to reduce the volume to
zero, and infinite volume to reduce the pressure to zero.
**What the other graphs represent.**
**Graph I**, horizontal: constant pressure - an **isobaric** process ✓
**Graph II**, rising line: P increasing with V, which needs the temperature to rise
steeply ✓
**Graph III**, falling line: P decreasing linearly - a possible process, but not at
constant T ✓
**Different isotherms.** Each temperature has its **own** hyperbola ✓ and the higher
the temperature the further from the origin, since PV = nRT is larger. A family of
non-intersecting hyperbolas fills the P-V plane.
**The adiabatic curve, for contrast.** PV^γ = constant, with γ = 1·4 for air ✓ It is
**steeper** than the isotherm through the same point, because an expanding gas also
**cools**, lowering the pressure further.
**The work done.** The area under the isotherm,
W = **nRT ln(V₂/V₁)** ✓ and since ΔU = 0 for an isothermal change, all of it comes from
heat absorbed.
**Where real gases depart.** Near condensation, Boyle's law fails and the isotherm
develops a **flat portion** where liquid and vapour coexist ✓ Above the critical
temperature the hyperbola is restored.
∴ Graph-IV.

Each beat count gives **two** possible frequencies; the right ν satisfies **both**.
**Step 1 — use the first beat count.** Six beats per second against 200 Hz means
ν = 200 ± 6
= **194 Hz or 206 Hz** ✓
**Step 2 — use the second.** The second harmonic, 2ν, gives 8 beats against 420 Hz:
2ν = 420 ± 8 = **412 or 428**
so
ν = **206 Hz or 214 Hz** ✓
**Step 3 — find the common value.** The only frequency appearing in both lists is
**206 Hz** ✓
**Step 4 — verify.**
|206 − 200| = **6 beats** ✓
2ν = 412, and |412 − 420| = **8 beats** ✓ both conditions met.
**Why one measurement is not enough.** The beat frequency gives only the **magnitude**
of the difference ✓ Whether the unknown is above or below the reference is left open,
which is why a second observation is needed to break the ambiguity.
**The practical method of resolving it.** **Load** the source slightly - adding wax to
a tuning fork lowers its frequency ✓ If the beats become **fewer**, the source was
above the reference; if **more**, below. Piano tuners use exactly this trick.
**What beats are.** The slow rise and fall in loudness when two close frequencies
superpose ✓
**f_beat = |f₁ − f₂|** ✓ and the amplitude modulates at that rate while the ear hears
the **mean** frequency.
**Why only a few beats per second are useful.** Above about 10 Hz the ear no longer
hears separate pulsations but a rough, unpleasant tone ✓ which is why tuning is done
by reducing the beats to zero.
**Where beats are used.** Tuning musical instruments, detecting small frequency
differences in the laboratory, and in the **heterodyne** receiver, where mixing two
frequencies produces a convenient intermediate one ✓
**The algebra behind them.**
sin ω₁t + sin ω₂t = 2 cos[(ω₁ − ω₂)t/2] sin[(ω₁ + ω₂)t/2] ✓
the slow cosine being the envelope and the fast sine the audible tone.
**Why the second harmonic is used here.** It doubles the unknown frequency, so a
6 Hz ambiguity at ν becomes a **12 Hz** separation at 2ν ✓ large enough that only one
of the original candidates can also satisfy the second condition.
**Reading the distractors.** **194 Hz** satisfies the first condition but gives
2ν = 388 and **32 beats** against 420 ✗ **205** and **210 Hz** ✗ satisfy neither ✓
∴ 206 Hz.

All four processes proceed spontaneously in **one direction only** - every one is
irreversible.
**Step 1 — test free expansion.** A gas rushing into a vacuum ✓ It never spontaneously
gathers itself back into one half of the vessel. The entropy increases by
nR ln 2 for a doubling, and the process is **irreversible**.
**Step 2 — test combustion.** Petrol and air burning to carbon dioxide and water ✓ The
products never recombine into fuel and oxygen of their own accord. **Irreversible**.
**Step 3 — test the gas leak.** Gas escaping from a cylinder disperses through the
room ✓ It never spontaneously returns and repressurises the cylinder.
**Irreversible**.
**Step 4 — test heat conduction.** Heat flowing from the hot part of a liquid to the
cold ✓ It never flows back unaided - that is the **Clausius statement** of the second
law. **Irreversible**.
**Step 5 — conclude.** **All four** ✓
**What makes a process reversible.** It must be **quasi-static** - infinitely slow, so
the system stays in equilibrium throughout - and **free of dissipation**: no friction,
no viscosity, no unrestrained expansion, no finite temperature difference ✓
**Why no real process qualifies.** Every one of those conditions is an idealisation ✓
Reversibility is a limiting case, approached but never reached - useful as a standard
against which real processes are measured.
**The entropy criterion.**
reversible: **ΔS_universe = 0** ✓
irreversible: **ΔS_universe > 0** ✓
Every one of the four processes increases the entropy of the universe, which is the
formal statement that they cannot run backwards.
**Why each is irreversible, in a word.**
free expansion: **unrestrained** - the gas does no work ✓
combustion: a **chemical** change releasing energy ✓
leaking gas: **unrestrained** again, plus mixing ✓
heat conduction: a **finite** temperature difference ✓
**The nearest approach to reversibility.** A very slow, frictionless, isothermal
expansion against an external pressure differing only infinitesimally from the gas's
own ✓ Such a process can be reversed at every stage by an infinitesimal change.
**Why the second law is so unlike the first.** The first law permits a process to run
either way; the **second** picks out a direction ✓ It is the only fundamental law that
distinguishes past from future.
**Reading the distractors.** Each selects a subset ✓ but all four processes fail the
test of reversibility, so none may be excluded.
∴ I, II, III and IV.

Work done in moving a charge equals **q(V_B − V_A)**.
**Step 1 — state the relation.**
W = q(V_B − V_A) ✓
**Step 2 — substitute.**
200 = 5[V − (−20)] ✓
**Step 3 — simplify.**
200 = 5(V + 20)
40 = V + 20 ✓
**Step 4 — solve.**
**V = 20 V** ✓
**Why the two minus signs matter.** V_A is **−20 V**, so subtracting it **adds** 20 ✓
Writing 5(V − 20) instead gives V = 60 - which is the fourth option, and the designed
trap.
**What the work represents.** The energy an external agent must supply to move the
charge **against** the electric force ✓ Here it is positive, so B is at a **higher**
potential than A - the charge is being pushed uphill.
**The potential difference.**
V_B − V_A = 20 − (−20) = **40 V** ✓
and W = qΔV = 5 x 40 = **200 J** ✓ confirming the answer.
**Why only the difference matters.** The absolute value of the potential depends on
where the zero is chosen ✓ Shifting both potentials by any amount leaves ΔV, and hence
the work, unchanged. That is why the choice of zero - usually at infinity, or at earth -
is a matter of convenience.
**Why the path is irrelevant.** The electric force is **conservative** ✓ so the work
depends only on the endpoints. A charge carried round a closed loop and back to A does
**zero** net work, however winding the route.
**A worked check in reverse.** Moving the same charge from B back to A:
W = 5(−20 − 20) = **−200 J** ✓ the agent now **recovers** 200 J, as it must.
**What the sign of the work tells us.**
**positive**: the external agent does work, the charge gains potential energy ✓
**negative**: the field does the work, and the charge loses potential energy ✓
**Why the charge is positive here.** A **negative** charge of 5 C would require
−200 J - that is, it would be pushed **spontaneously** from A to B ✓ The sign of q
reverses the whole picture.
**The energy in electron volts, for scale.** 200 J is enormous by atomic standards -
some 1·25 x 10²¹ eV ✓ a reminder that a coulomb is a vast quantity of charge.
**Reading the distractors.** **60 V** ✗ mishandles the double negative. **10 V** ✗ and
**40 V** ✗ correspond to works of 150 J and 300 J ✓
∴ 20 V.

Apply **Kirchhoff's current law** at each junction in turn.
**Step 1 — the first junction.** 5 A arrives from the left, and 1 A leaves down the
lower-left branch:
I₁ = 5 − 1
= **4 A** ✓
**Step 2 — the second junction.** I₁ = 4 A arrives, 1·5 A leaves to the right, and I₂
goes down:
I₂ = 4 − 1·5
= **2·5 A** ✓
**Step 3 — the third junction.** I₂ = 2·5 A arrives from above, 1·5 A leaves to the
right, and I₃ continues down:
I₃ = 2·5 − 1·5
= **1 A** ✓
**Step 4 — state the three.** **4 A, 2·5 A and 1 A** ✓
**The principle at work.** Kirchhoff's current law is **conservation of charge** ✓ No
charge accumulates at a junction in a steady circuit, so the total arriving equals the
total leaving.
**Why the junctions must be taken in order.** Each one's answer feeds the next ✓
Starting in the middle would leave two unknowns in a single equation.
**The sign convention.** Currents **into** a node positive, **out of** it negative,
and the sum zero ✓ Reading the arrow directions correctly is the only real difficulty -
a misread arrow propagates through every subsequent step.
**A check on the whole network.** Total in: **5 A** ✓ Total out: 1 + 1·5 + 1·5 + 1 =
**5 A** ✓ balanced, as conservation of charge demands. This global check is worth
making whenever the node-by-node work is finished.
**Why no resistances are given.** None is needed ✓ The current law constrains the
**currents** alone; resistances would be needed only to find how a current **divides**
between parallel branches, which here the diagram already specifies.
**The companion law.** Kirchhoff's **voltage** law: the sum of potential differences
round any closed loop is **zero** ✓ - conservation of energy, as the current law is
conservation of charge. Together they solve any network.
**Why charge cannot accumulate.** It would create a growing electric field that
immediately drove it away ✓ The adjustment happens in about 10⁻¹⁸ s in a conductor, so
for all practical purposes the law is exact.
**Where the laws were established.** Gustav Kirchhoff published them in **1845**, while
still a student ✓ They remain the foundation of all circuit analysis.
**Reading the distractors.** Each alternative fails the balance at one junction or
another ✓ Tracing the three nodes in order leaves no room for doubt.
∴ 4A, 2.5A and 1A.

Find the current from the power rating, then divide by the electronic charge.
**Step 1 — find the current.**
I = P/V
= 60/120
= **0·5 A** ✓
**Step 2 — convert to electrons per second.** Current is charge per second, and each
electron carries e:
n = I/e
= 0·5/(1·6 x 10⁻¹⁹) ✓
**Step 3 — evaluate.**
= **3·125 x 10¹⁸ ≈ 3·1 x 10¹⁸ per second** ✓
**What the number means.** Over three **billion billion** electrons pass each second ✓
and that is a modest 60 W lamp. The sheer count is why charge appears continuous in
every everyday measurement, though it is quantised at the deepest level.
**Why the electrons themselves move so slowly.** Their **drift velocity** is under a
millimetre per second ✓ There are simply so many of them - about 10²⁹ per cubic metre
in the filament - that a slow drift carries a large current.
**The charge transported.**
0·5 C per second ✓ and in an hour, 1800 C - which is about 1·1 x 10²² electrons.
**The filament's resistance.**
R = V/I = 120/0·5 = **240 Ω** when hot ✓ Cold, it would be perhaps twenty times
smaller, which is why a lamp draws a large surge at switch-on and usually fails at
that moment.
**Why the lamp is so inefficient.** The filament runs at about 2800 K, and by Wien's
law its emission peaks at **1·04 µm** - in the **infrared** ✓ Only some 5% of the 60 W
emerges as visible light; the rest is heat.
**A sense of scale for the current.** 0·5 A is typical for a lamp; a kettle draws about
**10 A**, and a lightning stroke some **30000 A** ✓
**Why charge quantisation is invisible here.** The granularity is one part in
3 x 10¹⁸ ✓ Detecting it requires either very small currents - as in shot-noise
measurements - or single-electron devices.
**Checking the units.**
[I/e] = (C s⁻¹)/C = **s⁻¹** ✓ a rate, as required.
**Reading the distractors.** **6·2 x 10¹⁸** ✗ is twice the answer, from using 1 A.
**6·2 x 10¹⁹** and **3·1 x 10¹⁹** ✗ are ten times too large ✓ The division
0·5/1·6 x 10⁻¹⁹ = 3·125 x 10¹⁸ settles it.
∴ 3.1 × 10¹⁸.
